extracted.intended_audience: reporters, city editors, and journalism students writing accident/fire news stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and structuring accident and fire news stories: how to write leads, casualty lists, body structure, handling details, tone, and newsroom-friendly formatting for quick revisions. Focuses on clarity, specificity, chronology choices, and ethical/taste considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where and When are imperatives for the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where" and "When" are imperatives for the lead to a fire story, because they are the first questions readers ask when they see a fire headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always answer where and when early in the lead so readers immediately place the event. Example: contrast '1632 Grand Avenue' (insufficient alone) with '65 Elm Street, directly across the street from Hotel Warren.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific in identifying location
rubrics_metrics.description: A more complete identification is desirable; include landmarks, cross streets, and both present and former names of venerable buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give enough context so readers can find the spot within several blocks. Example: 'The Central Building, formerly the Cranston Block, at 305 Sauk Street.' Include former names for older readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must state casualties and seriousness; put life before property
rubrics_metrics.description: The first two requisites of a fire story lead are to tell whether anyone was killed or hurt and then give a definite concept of the seriousness of the blaze. Regardless of property damage, loss of life is mentioned before property damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always lead with human impact if any (e.g., 'One man was burned to death...') even if property loss is large. This is an ethical and audience-priority rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make magnitude visualizable rather than relying on dollar amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may not visualize sums like $50,000 or $100,000; find expressions that can be more easily visualized than money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative or descriptive images (e.g., 'fire that menaced an entire business block', 'a blaze that roared for five hours', 'scorched paint on buildings half a block away') to convey scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hyperbolic rhetoric and melodrama; use loaded words sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Striving for vivid phrasing is good, but reporters should avoid terrible overwrought language or worn-out cliches. Use words like 'conflagration' sparingly and only when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the blaze was not massive, don't strain the rhetoric. 'Conflagration' should be reserved for fires sweeping a wide area (three or four blocks). Avoid flamboyant metaphors (e.g., 'great red demon...') that mislead or sound ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and accurately use local alarm terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrasings such as 'two-alarm fire' and 'general-alarm blaze' vary in power from city to city and sometimes within a city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand local fire-department practices so you don't overstate or misrepresent the seriousness. Recognize that some departments overuse alarms and that 'general alarm' has operational and insurance implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid about uncertainty rather than manufacturing a definitive outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid past-era practices of writing so a story 'will fit whichever way the fire turns out.' Today, editors prefer frank statements of uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If outcome is unknown at press time, state that (e.g., 'at press time it was uncertain whether the building could be saved') instead of asserting a premature result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show specifics rather than vague virtues ('show, don't tell')
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalized words like 'bravery' or 'presence of mind' are weak because they cannot be visualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the concrete actions that demonstrate the virtue. Example: instead of 'presence of mind,' write how a policeman ran to a garage and inflated an inner tube to use as a life preserver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tasteless humor and manufactured tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't be funny about incidents that are inherently serious, nor try to create undue tragedy out of minor happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect victims; avoid jokey leads about lost pets or melodramatic tear-jerkers that the generality of readers will resent. An occasional genuinely humorous accident may be reported, but treat it with taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of victims: civilians and passengers before officers/crew
rubrics_metrics.description: Deaths 'in the line of duty' (fireman, policeman, crew) are less newsworthy than civilian deaths; accident leads mention civilians and passengers before officers and crew members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place civilian casualties before service personnel unless circumstances are extraordinary; recognize the newsroom mores that guide this ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the casualty list immediately after the lead (or use a flash lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the nature of the lead, the casualty list follows it at once. Readers want to know at a glance who was killed or injured and whether they know any of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes the casualty list is run first after the headline or presented as a flash/skeleton lead followed by the list and then the completed lead. Use judgment based on length and prominence of the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph each casualty's name separately for clarity and ease of revision
rubrics_metrics.description: The much preferred procedure is to paragraph each name (killed first, then injured).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate paragraphs give each name prominence and allow simple 'pulling' and revision when statuses change. Use boldface or distinctive typography per copy-editor directions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe hospital and official qualifiers scrupulously
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever qualifications the hospital makes in describing injuries are to be observed scrupulously (e.g., 'probable fractured skull').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overrule medical qualifiers based on reporter assumptions; incorrect assertion can bring reprisal from sources and damage credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep casualty lists current—changes can happen quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: A casualty list must be kept up to date. Changes can occur within a few minutes (e.g., 'resting comfortably' may become 'dead').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor updates closely and design copy/paragraphing to permit quick revision without retyping large sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short paragraphs and block structure to facilitate revisions and typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because later information changes so many accident stories, writing must be meticulously realistic so revisions can be made quickly. The story is split into short paragraphs so that an amendment affects only a few lines of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide action so each phase/aspect has a separate paragraph; avoid long transitions and linking words that lock paragraphs together (e.g., 'Meanwhile,' 'At the same time,'). Short blocks also allow multiple compositors to work and guard against paragraph-reordering problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transitions that tightly link paragraphs unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions are tabu unless coherence makes them inescapable because they link paragraphs too closely and can lead to gibberish if paragraph order is changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitions only when required for understanding. Favor self-contained blocks that remain coherent even if shuffled in typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one of three main story structures: chronological, reverse chronology, or dwindling-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The accident story may have one of three structures: chronological, reverse chronology, or dwindling-interest. One lead will suffice for all three methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chronological for straightforward, easy-to-follow accounts (good when sprinting with the clock). Use reverse chronology when the final action is truly decisive and you have time to craft it carefully. Use dwindling-interest (most-preferred) to put the most important details up front and then decrease importance—requires competent writing and clear analysis of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the lead's sequence when elaborating details
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a lead introduces details, or where it is several paragraphs long, the elaboration of the details follows the order of their mention in the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the lead as a framework; present details in the same sequence so readers can tack details onto the lead's frame. Numbering or block labeling can help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle simultaneous actions by summarizing then detailing, or by combining actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing concurrent actions can be difficult. The reporter has two methods: (1) write a paragraph summarizing the various simultaneous actions, then describe each in detail in separate paragraphs in the order forecasted; (2) combine the actions into a single (possibly long) paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which method best preserves clarity. The summary-plus-details method keeps blocks distinct; the combined paragraph may be acceptable when brevity is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group gruesome details into one section near the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Gruesome details should be herded into one section of the story, as near the end as possible, rather than diffused throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating gruesome detail protects nervous readers from repeated emotional assaults and keeps the main narrative more readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roundup stories: mirror the lead order and consider a block arrangement when one accident dominates
rubrics_metrics.description: The roundup, grouping a series of accidents into one comprehensive story, demands that the body present the accidents in the sequence given in the lead. If one accident is much more newsworthy, use block structures (summaries then details) as suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two block arrangements are recommended: (a) summary of most newsworthy accident, summary of others, then details of lead accident, then details of others; (b) summary of all accidents with lead first, then details of lead, then details of lesser accidents. Choose based on relative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and stale phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The cliche does more than any other factor to make accident stories deadly alike. Avoid stock phrases like 'belching billows of smoke', 'angry waters', 'narrow escape', or misapplied terms like 'crack train' for any wrecked train.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for fresh, specific language. Clichés make stories feel alike and reduce impact; editors and readers notice and may lampoon malapropisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place background material appropriately: brief background after casualty list; long background split or separate
rubrics_metrics.description: Background is largely explaining that the new accident is one of a series or has distinctive elements. If the background is brief, it often is run immediately after the casualty list; if not, split it into 'lead background' and full background at the end, or run the background as a separate adjoining story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep main report tight; use background to explain context but avoid cluttering the lead or casualty details if the background is lengthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the story interesting by finding vivid details and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the accident story interesting is principally a matter of finding out its details. A flash or two of dialog often will do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct (lively) quotes rather than bland paraphrase when possible; include sidelight facts that show reporter dug deep (e.g., repeated injuries to a hoseman) to add authority and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-day stories require a summary of the original first-day account
rubrics_metrics.description: Many accidents are news for more than one day. Later accounts require a summary of the original story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When updating, begin with a concise recap of key facts from the first-day story before giving new developments, investigations, or changes in the casualty list.
